label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Here's your reply to Bergeron. I kept it in your voice — straight, a bit warm, no fighting — and put all the facts in there.

---

Hello everyone — Hélène Gagnon here, owner of Le Pétrin Doré, 5 rue Fairmount (the corner). D. Bergeron, you asked for a straight answer before the 4th, so here it is, all of it, and I'm sorry to make you wait for it until now.

**The short version: we are not closing. We bought the building.**

I know how that reads. I read this thread myself for the first time on Saturday morning (my nephew showed it to me and I was, let's say, not happy), and I understand the worry. Mile End has lost a lot of small shops and nobody wants another one. So let me explain everything, in order, and then you can judge.

**1. The building.** The whole building — the ground floor commercial space and the three apartments above it — was sold. To me. Signed at the notary on December 15. I am the new owner.

Marc-Antoine, your cousin is half right. The building was sold. Just not to a developer, not to a bank, and not to a vape shop. To the woman who has been baking in the ground floor of it since March 2009.

M. Ferland is 81 and he's retiring to Sherbrooke with his daughter. He could have sold to anybody — the market was there, and I am sure there were bigger names interested. But he offered it to me first, because he knows what this corner means, and because he knows that I would keep the bakery and keep the flats above it. He cried a little at the notary. He came every morning for 17 years for his baguette — pas trop cuite, he said, every single morning — and he will have to get used to eating it in his own kitchen now. I owe him more than I can say in a post.

**2. The sign.** Yes, that sign is my fault. My nephew Thomas wrote it at 6 in the morning, before I was even awake. The "Grande nouvelle bientôt!" was his idea and I said "ok" without thinking. I wanted to keep the surprise for the reopening — the new oven, the new tables in the back, and now this — but a sign like that on a door reads like a threat, and I should have written something clearer. That's on me, and I'm sorry. There was no big news coming that would have hurt anybody. The big news is good news.

**3. The half-empty shelves on the 28th.** We sold everything for Christmas Eve — 400 bûches, made by hand, and they go in a morning. That's all that was. It wasn't a sign of anything except a very good Christmas Eve.

**4. The two weeks.** We close Monday January 4 and reopen Tuesday January 19 at 7 a.m. We were closed for two weeks because of works, and the main one is a new deck oven with four decks, coming from our supplier in Laval. The old oven is from 1998 and it broke three times this year. Every time it broke, I lost a morning of production and a night of sleep, and I stopped being able to promise people their bread on the day they wanted it.

The second thing: we are taking the back space — the old dépanneur storage — and we're putting six small tables there. Six. So people can finally sit down. Right now you have to stand at the counter with your coffee like you're waiting for a bus, and I have wanted to fix that for years. Some of the work is done, some isn't, that's the other reason for the closure.

**5. Come to the reopening.** Tuesday January 19, 7 a.m., first loaf out of the new oven. I'll be there at 6:15.

And then, for the party: **Saturday January 23**, from 8 a.m. Coffee and a piece of the new bread, free, for everyone. Regulars, neighbours, people who came once, people who only ever walked by, and all of you on this board who were kind enough to worry about us. Come see the new oven and sit at the new tables. Bring your kids, Priya, your kid knows where the chocolatines are.

**6. The carnets.** This is the important part, so I'm going to be very clear.

We sold 214 carnets in October, $60 for 12 loaves. Every single one of them is honoured. There is no expiry. The 12 loaves are waiting for you and the bread doesn't care that we took two weeks off — you come in, you get your bread. And in January, every carnet holder gets a free croissant. That's a promise, and I don't make promises I can't keep.

And since I know what some of you were thinking (noodle_and_crumb, I'm talking to you — you were honest, I appreciate it): if you really want your money back for your carnet, come into the shop and I will give it back to you. No question, no conditions, no awkwardness, no hard feelings. I would much rather have the doubters inside the door than outside it. But I don't want to have to do that, because 214 people handed me their money in good faith in October and that is a thing I keep, not a thing I cash in and run on.

And for the record: a scam? After 17 years on this street, that one hurt. I'm not going to argue with anybody on this board. I'm going to say it once and then I'd like to move on: this is my life, my ovens, my bread, my neighbours, the same corner since 2009. I bake every morning. I know half of you by name and I know what your kids like. That's not something you can fake and then disappear with in January.

**7. The three apartments upstairs.** They stay rented. Same tenants, same rent, same leases, nothing changes. And I'm putting it in writing — I'm sending each of them a signed letter saying exactly that. If any of you live upstairs and you were worried: you are not losing your home because I bought the building. Nothing changes for you. And for the neighbours who were worried about the apartments, nothing changes there either.

**8. Thank you.** To Priya, who knew me when I didn't need to be defended, and to everyone else who said out loud that this might not be what it looked like — thank you. Priya, your Saturday chocolatines are not forgotten either, don't think for a second they are.

I know the street has had enough surprises to last. I bought this building because I wanted the bakery to still be here, and the flats above it to still be there, and because I'd rather have a two-week closure and a new oven than watch another corner become a vape shop. That was the "grande nouvelle". It was supposed to be announced in person, with coffee, in a good mood.

Now I have to tell you with my fingers on a keyboard, so: no condo, no bank, no closing. We're staying. Reopen January 19 at 7 a.m., party on January 23, coffee's on me.

See you on the 19th.

— Hélène

---

A couple of small things to check before you post: I put "8 a.m." for the January 23 hours — change it to whatever hour you want people to show up. And I signed it "Hélène" without "Gagnon" since Bergeron already called you Mme Gagnon; add it if you'd rather. Want me to make a shorter version for the board too, in case people don't scroll?
